options: A policy attached directly to a resource (like an S3 bucket), naming which principals can access it
A policy attached to an IAM user that lists which resources they own
A policy that only applies to EC2 instances
A synonym for a trust policy on an IAM role
questions.explain: A resource-based policy (like an S3 bucket policy) is attached to the resource itself and specifies which principals may access it — the opposite attachment point from an identity-based policy.

questions.q: Why must a bucket policy's JSON include a Principal field, unlike a typical identity-based policy?
options: Because the policy isn't attached to an identity, so it must explicitly name who it applies to
Because bucket policies apply to every AWS account automatically
Principal is optional in bucket policies just like identity policies
Because S3 requires a different JSON syntax entirely from IAM
questions.explain: Since a resource-based policy is attached to the resource rather than an identity, it must name the Principal(s) it grants or denies access to.

questions.q: If an identity policy allows s3:GetObject and the bucket policy is silent (says nothing) about that role, is access granted?
options: Yes — one Allow from either the identity policy or bucket policy is enough, absent any explicit Deny
No — both policies must explicitly allow the same action
No — silence from the bucket policy is treated as an explicit Deny
It depends on which AWS region the bucket is in
questions.explain: AWS evaluates all applicable policies together; an Allow from either the identity policy or the resource policy is sufficient when no explicit Deny is present.

questions.q: An identity policy allows s3:GetObject, but the bucket policy has an explicit Deny for the same role. What happens?
options: Access is denied — an explicit Deny in any applicable policy always overrides any Allow
Access is granted because the identity policy takes precedence
AWS averages the two policies and grants partial access
The request fails with an error rather than being allowed or denied
questions.explain: An explicit Deny in any applicable policy — identity-based or resource-based — always overrides any Allow, no matter where that Allow comes from.

questions.q: Which of these is a real reason to use a bucket policy instead of relying solely on identity policies?
options: Granting a different AWS account access to your bucket
Bucket policies are required for every S3 bucket by default
Identity policies cannot grant s3:GetObject under any circumstances
Bucket policies replace the need for IAM roles entirely
questions.explain: A bucket policy is often necessary specifically for granting access to principals outside the identities you manage directly — most commonly another AWS account, as covered in the cross-account access lesson.
